abstract.text:
We consider the problem of fast time-series data clustering. Building on previous work modeling the correlation-based Hamiltonian of spin variables we present an updated fast non-expensive
Agglomerative Likelihood Clustering algorithm (ALC). The method replaces the optimized genetic
algorithm based approach (f-SPC) with an agglomerative recursive merging framework inspired by
previous work in Econophysics and Community Detection. The method is tested on noisy synthetic
correlated time-series data-sets with built-in cluster structure to demonstrate that the algorithm
produces meaningful non-trivial results. We apply it to time-series data-sets as large as 20,000 assets and we argue that ALC can reduce compute time costs and resource usage cost for large scale
clustering for time-series applications while being serialized, and hence has no obvious parallelization requirement. The algorithm can be an effective choice for state-detection for online learning in
a fast non-linear data environment because the algorithm requires no prior information about the
number of clusters.

sections.summary: Motivates fast unsupervised clustering for large, nonstationary financial time-series and introduces Agglomerative Likelihood Clustering as a serialized, non-expensive alternative to f-SPC. The paper positions ALC against threshold-based network approaches, emphasizes dense correlation matrices, no prior cluster count, and a roadmap through model, algorithm, synthetic tests, bootstrap, hierarchical blocks, and performance.
sections.title: Introduction: Fast Time-Series Clustering with ALC

sections.summary: Introduces the Noh ansatz and Giada-Marsili spin Hamiltonian as the cluster likelihood. Defines a generative model where each feature combines cluster influence, node-specific effect, and intra-cluster coupling. Derives log-likelihood Lc in terms of cluster sizes ns and intra-cluster correlations cs, and argues it depends only on the correlation matrix and is adaptive to cluster number.
sections.title: Giada-Marsili Likelihood Model

source_span.end_text: Tables II and III initialization and main routine

sections.summary: Presents ALC as a bottom-up greedy merging algorithm. It contrasts PGA issues with a Louvain-inspired tracker-based merge search. The algorithm uses the more restrictive Case 2 change in likelihood, computes individual-cluster Lc, and iteratively merges while maximizing positive Delta Lc.
sections.title: Agglomerative Likelihood Clustering Algorithm

sections.summary: Tests ALC on uncorrelated white-noise and correlated Student-t synthetic data. Uncorrelated data still yields small noise clusters, while correlated data vary by N, D, and gs. ARI tables compare ALC and HDBSCAN; ALC improves as clusters densify but degrades at low gs, short series, and large N.
sections.title: Synthetic Data Experiments and ARI Evaluation

sections.summary: Addresses low signal-to-noise ratio Q = D/N by resampling subsets and building a filtered correlation matrix. It defines pairwise co-occurrence fij, clustered-together frequency dij, probability pij, and ordinal threshold pωij. Experiments compare thresholds 0.5 and 0.75; 0.75 is superior, and larger n helps when q is fixed.
sections.title: Noise Handling via Bootstrap and Filtered Correlation

sections.summary: Extends evaluation to nested block correlation structures generated by multiple hierarchical factors. ALC and HDBSCAN recover nested clusters at low noise, but as cluster-specific noise alpha rises HDBSCAN labels observations as noise or merges clusters earlier. ALC is more robust, prioritizes smaller denser clusters, and starts degrading around alpha > 0.4.
sections.title: Hierarchical Block Correlations and HDBSCAN Comparison

sections.summary: Compares ALC runtime and solution quality with f-SPC and HDBSCAN. ALC consistently yields higher likelihood than f-SPC and runs roughly quadratically, while HDBSCAN is faster but less robust in some noisy settings. Discussion emphasizes serial operation, no cluster-number input, online-learning suitability, and future work on distributions, similarity measures, and Louvain-like optimizations.
sections.title: Performance, Runtime, and Conclusions

sections.summary: Bibliography of cited work. Optional navigation unit; lists clustering, econophysics, random matrix theory, HDBSCAN, Louvain, portfolio optimization, and related references.
sections.title: References

sections.summary: Provides ALC pseudocode that generates candidates, evaluates Lc, and selects best candidates. Appendix B details the Noh-ansatz synthetic data generator: cluster number C, cluster size s, time-series length D, spin labels, random effects eta and epsilon, intra-cluster binding gs, and returns via Eq B1. UMAP visualizations show how gs and series length affect cluster density.
sections.title: Appendices: ALC Pseudocode and Synthetic Data Generation
